en: The Apadāna of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya Bhaddiya Chapter 8 The Apadāna of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya: In the past, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kassapa appeared in the world, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Fortunate One. At that time, I was a forest-dwelling monk, living in the wilderness. Seeing the Teacher, the Great Sage, I approached him and paid homage. Having paid homage to the Teacher, the Great Sage, I sat down to one side. As I sat there, I spoke these words to the Teacher: "I am one who dwells in the forest; may I receive the higher ordination from you, O Blessed One. Then the Teacher, the Great Sage, out of compassion for me, granted me the higher ordination. Having received the higher ordination from the Teacher, the Great Sage, I practiced the holy life under the guidance of the Teacher, the Great Sage. Having spent twenty thousand years practicing the holy life under the guidance of the Teacher, the Great Sage, I passed away from that state and was reborn in the Brahma-world. From there, passing away, I was reborn in the human world. There, too, I was ordained as a monk and practiced the holy life. “In this auspicious eon,
there was one of great fame, a kinsman of Brahmā,
Kassapa by name as his clan.”
The best among those who debate appeared.
At that time, I was Candana,
and having gone forth into the Teaching;
Having fulfilled the Dhamma to the end of life within the Teaching,
upon passing away from there, he was reborn in the Santusita heaven.
We both have been reborn there,
amidst divine dances,
songs, and instrumental music.
Having surpassed all others by means of the eight factors beginning with physical beauty,
and having lived for the full span of his life,
Having experienced great bliss,
he passed away from there and was reborn among the Thirty-three gods as Candana.
I was born in Kapilavatthu, a scion of the Sakyans;
when by the Elder Udāyin—
Requested by the Leader of the World,
out of compassion for the Sakyans,
he went to Kapilavatthu.
At that time, the Sakyans were excessively proud and did not recognize the Buddha’s virtues;
they did not bow down to the Fully Awakened One.
Stubborn in their birth-status and disrespectful,
the Jina, having understood their intention,
walked back and forth in the air.
He rained like the rain-god Pajjunna and blazed like a fire;
having displayed his incomparable form, he departed.
Again you vanished;
having been one, you became many,
and then once more you became one.
Having displayed darkness and light in many ways,
and having performed a miracle,
The Sage, having disciplined his kinsmen,
[spoke thus]: "Let a great cloud rain down upon the four continents for just that long."
For at that time, the Buddha taught the Vessantara Jātaka;
at that time, all those kṣatriyas—
"Having destroyed the intoxication born of birth,
they have gone for refuge to the Buddha," Suddhodana then said.
“This is the third time, O one of vast wisdom,
that I bow at your feet, O all-seeing one;
when you were born, the earth trembled.”
And when that shade of the rose-apple tree did not leave him,
then, having seen that power of the Buddha,
his mind was filled with wonder.
Having gone forth right there,
I dwelt as one who honors his mother;
the divine son Candana [honored] me.
Having approached him,
inquire then about the method of the "One Fortunate Night" both in brief and in detail.
Then, having approached that Leader of Men, I was exhorted by him;
and having heard the "One Fortunate Night" discourse, I—
Filled with spiritual urgency, I went to the forest.
Then I asked my mother,
“I shall go to the forest alone.”
‘He is very delicate,’ my mother said,
and then she spoke these words to him:
“Do not go to the kāsa, the kusa, or the poṭakila [grasses].”
I shall push aside the usīra grass, the muñja grass,
and the pabbaja grass with my chest,
cultivating seclusion.
Then, having entered the forest and recalled the teaching of the Victor,
I remembered the instruction on the "Single Excellent Night."
I attained arahantship.
“One should not pursue the past,
nor long for the future;”
That which is past is abandoned;
that which is future has not yet been reached;
and as for the phenomenon of the present—
Therein he sees with insight;
the wise one should cultivate that which is unshakable and unshakeable.
"Today itself one should exert oneself in what is to be done;
who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For we have no appointment with it."
By Death with his great army.
One who dwells thus,
ardent and untiring by day and night—
"That indeed is called 'the one fortunate night' by the peaceful Sage.
My defilements have been incinerated.
I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me!
... [as before] ... the Buddha's teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) have been attained.
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed did the venerable elder Lomasakaṅgiya speak these verses.
The legend of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya is the eighth.
